title: Coming in 2027: Apple’s $1,000 home robot for FaceTime and switching on lights
gist: Per The Information, Apple under new CEO John Ternus is developing a roaming AI home robot (code-named J595, possibly 'HomeView Ultra') priced around $1,000+ targeting 2027, possibly slipping to 2028. Ars argues its reported features look underwhelming versus existing smart-home devices, with a tiny robotics team, though a limited-purpose robot is safer than a general-purpose one.

insights.claim: Apple is reportedly developing an AI-driven roaming home robot, code-named J595, that supports FaceTime calls and switches lights on when a person enters a room.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Apple is extending its smart-home push into mobile robotics.

insights.claim: Apple is reportedly aiming to launch the home robot at $1,000 or more by 2027, though development delays could push the launch to 2028.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A premium-priced consumer robot from Apple could arrive within 1-2 years, with slip risk.
insights.quote: aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027

insights.claim: The robot may be branded HomeView Ultra, in line with Apple's new HomeView stationary smart display.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Robot would sit atop an Apple home hub product line.

insights.claim: New Apple CEO John Ternus is pushing household robotics, backing both the roaming robot and a separate project for robots doing household tasks like folding clothes.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Robotics appears to be a strategic priority of Apple's new leadership.

insights.claim: The laundry-folding project would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators, but it is unclear whether Apple aims to build a general-purpose humanoid like 1X and Figure AI.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Potential future Apple entry into the humanoid-robot race against startups.

insights.claim: Apple's robotics effort reportedly has only about 10 'true roboticists', with many original engineers having left, versus a software team of roughly 300 people.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Thin hardware robotics talent is a key execution risk for the program.

insights.claim: The home robot project dates to prototypes from 2018 approved by former CEO Tim Cook, and engineers have spent years trying to make it more than a 'fancy way to make FaceTime calls' to justify a high price.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: An eight-year development with unclear use case suggests product-market-fit struggle.

insights.claim: The robot's reported features look underwhelming compared with existing smart home devices or even a robot vacuum, which has a clearer household use case.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Demand for a $1,000+ roaming FaceTime/lights robot is questionable.
insights.locator: However, the robot’s few reported features

insights.claim: A limited-purpose home robot makes more technical and safety sense today than a general-purpose autonomous robot that poses greater risks near humans; the open question is whether enough customers will pay for it.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Apple is trading capability for safety; commercial success hinges on pricing and willingness to pay.
insights.quote: The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot.
